It's a small glass case on the second floor. And inside it is one fine gold necklace.

That necklace belonged to Edith Vanderbilt. George's wife. She wore it every single day for the last 44 years of her life.

Here's the story, and I promise it goes somewhere I did not expect.

Edith Stuyvesant Dresser married George Vanderbilt in 1898. They had one daughter, Cornelia. They lived in that 250-room house on 125,000 acres. They hosted presidents. They threw the kind of parties you read about in Edith Wharton novels.

In March of 1914, George died. He was 51. She was 40.

Edith outlived him by 44 years. She died in December of 1958.

And around her neck for every single one of those 44 years was a fine gold chain with a pattern of tiny gold beads and thin gold lines running along it.

For years, tourists have stopped in front of that glass case and asked me what the pattern meant.

And I used to tell them the same thing everyone told me when I started the job. That it was a decorative Gilded Age piece. That Edith just liked the design.

I was wrong. Very wrong.

I found out because of a tour I gave last February.

There was an older woman toward the back of the group. Well dressed. Quiet. She kept looking at that case longer than everyone else. After the tour ended and the group scattered, she came up to me.

She told me her name and I recognized it. She is one of Edith Vanderbilt's great-granddaughters. She said she comes to walk through the house alone maybe once a year.

She pointed at the necklace in the case and said, "You know what those beads spell, don't you?"

I said no.

She unbuttoned the top button of her shirt and pulled out a fine gold necklace of her own. Almost identical to the one in the case. Small beads. Thin lines. Delicate.

"Morse code," she said. "The one in the case says George Vanderbilt's full name. Edith had it made about a year after he died. She had one made for each of her daughters and granddaughters over the years. Mine is her name, and my husband's. He passed in 2019."

She said Edith wore hers because she could not bear another day of women grabbing her hands at social functions with wet eyes, asking her how she was getting on. She said her great-grandmother once told her sister that after George died, being a widow in public was like being pulled apart every time she left the house. And the necklace was the only thing she had ever found that let her keep him with her without paying that toll.

She said the tradition never actually died. It just went quiet.

I asked her, a little embarrassed, if it was something you could still get made.

She smiled. She said her granddaughter had ordered hers from a brand called Tulas. That they hand-code any name, any date, any message you want into Morse code along a fine gold chain. That from the outside it looks like ordinary jewelry. That nobody in the world can read it but the person wearing it.

She said, "It's the same thing Edith wore. We just call it a different name now."

That sentence sat in my stomach the rest of the day.

I went home that night and looked them up expecting the necklace to be $5,000.

But to my absolute surprise they were less than what I spend every time I refuel my car.

The chain is 14k gold-filled. It doesn't tarnish. The clasp is small and tight and doesn't loosen. The beads are welded to the chain so nothing slips off. You can shower in it, sleep in it, swim in it, wear it every day for the rest of your life.

The exact spec of the piece in the glass case, made today.

I ordered one for myself.

My father died eight months ago. He was 71. He had a heart attack on a Sunday morning sitting in his chair in the living room with the newspaper on his lap, the way he did every Sunday morning of my entire childhood. He was just there and then he wasn't. No warning. No goodbye.

My dad was not a famous man. He was not a Vanderbilt. He drove a school bus for thirty-one years. He coached Little League even though he wasn't very good at baseball and the kids all knew it and he didn't care. He built a deck behind our house the summer I was twelve and it took him four weekends and every board was slightly crooked and it was the most beautiful thing I had ever seen.

He called me his best girl.

From the time I was small until the last time I saw him. Every phone call. Every time he saw me walk through the door. Every Sunday morning when I called to check in and he picked up on the first ring without fail for thirty-five years.

His best girl.

When he died, nobody called me that anymore. I didn't realize until a few weeks after the funeral how much of myself lived in that phrase. How much of the day I had spent without knowing it waiting to hear it. You don't know what a thing means to you until the person who said it is gone and the silence where it used to be is louder than anything else.

She couldn't carry George. She couldn't take the 250 rooms with her. She couldn't bring the house. But she could take one small thing that said his name in a language nobody else could read. I put it on and looked in the mirror and there was nothing to see. Just a necklace.

And I stood there with my hand pressed flat over it and I cried. And it was the first time in eight months that crying felt like it was doing something instead of just happening to me.

Because he was right there. Not gone. Not in a sympathy card or on an order of service. Just there. His best girl. Same as always.

I wear it every day now. I shower in it. I sleep in it. The gold never tarnishes, never fades. It just stays. Which is everything I needed.

A woman on one of my tours last week told me she loved my necklace.

I said thank you.

I did not explain.

And I stood there in front of Edith Vanderbilt's glass case with my hand on my chest and my dad right there under my fingers while she moved on to ask about the paintings, and I just smiled and nodded and didn't say a single word.

Because for eight months the only two options I had were say nothing and carry it alone, or say something and watch someone's face go to that place where they don't know what to do.

She put it on that night. She has not taken it off since.

His jacket is still on the hook. His glasses are still on the table. His book is still open.

bodyText:
My daughter-in-law asked me to take my necklace off at her baby shower. A year later, at her second one, she asked me where I got the one I was wearing.

Her name is Rachel. She married my son Paul four years ago. I like her, I have always liked her, but there has been this thing between us since the beginning, and I have never been able to name it exactly.

When she got pregnant, we were all thrilled. My first grandchild. Paul called me crying, actual tears, and I sat in my kitchen with the phone against my ear and just listened to my son cry happy tears about his baby.

The shower was in October, at Rachel's mother's house in Connecticut, a two-hour drive for me. I spent three weeks finding the right outfit. A navy dress, low heels, and the gold locket Paul's father gave me for our twenty-fifth anniversary, two years before he died. I had worn it three times since the funeral.

I wanted to look nice for my son's wife, for my future grandchild, for a photo I would probably frame.

I arrived early and helped set up, and Rachel hugged me at the door.

An hour into the shower, she pulled me aside in the hallway near the bathroom.

"Hey, can I ask you something real quick?"

"Of course."

"I'm just worried about the photos. Would you mind taking the necklace off? It's a bit much for the soft tones in here, and I want everyone to match."

My hand went to the locket before I could stop it.

"Oh. Okay."

"It's nothing personal. It's just the photographer."

Everyone. She wasn't asking everyone.

I walked to the bathroom, locked the door, and looked at myself in the mirror. The locket wasn't much. It was there. It was the only thing on me that wasn't trying to blend into the wall.

I unhooked the clasp and put it in my handbag.

My neck looked bare and old, and I looked like a woman who had just been told to disappear a little.

I came back out, I smiled, I managed half a mini quiche, and I got in my car at three and cried the whole drive home.

I did not wear a necklace for a year after that.

Not to Thanksgiving. Not to my granddaughter Lily's birth in December, or to Christmas at the hospital, or to Easter, or to her christening in May. Not once.

My jewelry box stayed shut on my dresser, and I stopped opening it.

It went further than necklaces. I started reading Rachel's texts twice before I answered them. I started dressing for other people's photos. I walked into every family dinner already half apologizing, for my earrings, for my laugh, for taking up a chair.

I am sixty-one years old, and a thirty-four-year-old had told me I was a bit much, and I had believed her.

Paul called me in September. Rachel's second shower was in two weeks, in October again. They had announced the second baby quietly, no big reveal, just the shower.

"Mom, I really want you there."

"Of course, honey. I'll be there."

I already knew I wasn't going to wear a necklace.

The Friday before the shower, I was at lunch with my friend Donna. We have known each other since our kids were in preschool. Her son is in California now, and she is alone too, mostly.

She was wearing something at her throat I could not stop looking at. A small silver knot, three open loops made of a single line, with a tiny purple heart in the middle of it.

"Donna, what is that?"

She touched it and laughed.

"It's a Celtic trinity knot. Some people call it the witch knot. I've had it on for three months."

"What is it for?"

"People wear it for protection, or for luck, or to keep other people's negativity away from them. That last one is why I wear it. You know how my sister-in-law is at dinner. She hasn't changed. But for three months, whatever she says has stayed on her side of the table. It doesn't reach me anymore."

I must have gone quiet, because she put her fork down.

"Carol, I've watched you fade since last October, a little more every time I've seen you. First the necklaces went, then the earrings, then you stopped doing your hair to have lunch with me. It wasn't the locket Rachel wanted gone, it was you, and you've been doing it for her ever since."

Then she pointed at the little heart.

"That's February, my birthstone. You get it in your own month, and the protection is stronger."

I asked her where she had found it.

"It's the Witch Knot Birthstone Necklace, from Avera."

I ordered it that night from my kitchen table, in January, my month. There was an offer on, so a second one came with it, and I chose December for that one, Lily's month, and put it away for when she is older.

It arrived on Wednesday. The shower was Saturday.

I took it out of the box in my bathroom. It was even lighter than it had looked on Donna, a little open silver knot with a dark red heart in the middle. I fastened it, and it sat just below the hollow of my throat.

In the bathroom light the crystal behind the knot looked almost black. I walked to the window, and it turned nearly turquoise.

I stood there for probably two minutes, just looking. I did not look dressed up. I looked awake. I looked like the photo of me and Paul's father from 1989 that sits on my dresser.

Saturday morning, I put it on at seven before I drove to Connecticut. I got there at ten, and the shower started at eleven.

Rachel opened the door and hugged me.

"You look great, Carol."

"Thank you."

She didn't pull me aside. She didn't say anything about the photographer.

Her mother did, in passing, by the buffet.

"Oh, a necklace this time."

I heard myself laugh, and I meant it. The remark was there, and then it was still there, on her, and not on me.

I watched Rachel throughout the shower. She was glowing, second pregnancy, visibly exhausted, but happy. Her mother was there, her sisters, her friends from college. Her mother and I were the only two women over fifty in the room.

I sat on the couch with a cucumber sandwich and watched my son rub her back every time she stood up. I watched Lily, ten months old, crawl at full speed around her own mother's chair. Paul used to do that, in our old kitchen.

And I thought about all the months I had spent with my jewelry box shut because a thirty-four-year-old had made me feel like too much.

Around two, Rachel sat down next to me on the couch.

"Carol, can I ask you something?"

I stiffened. I don't know why. Muscle memory, maybe.

"Of course."

"Where did you get that necklace? It's beautiful."

I looked at her. She wasn't asking me to take it off. She was asking me where I got it.

"It's called the Witch Knot Birthstone Necklace, from Avera. The heart is my birthstone. Lily has one waiting for her in her month, for when she's older."

She nodded slowly.

"It's really pretty on you."

"Thank you, Rachel."

She sat there for a second. Then she said, and I am quoting her exactly, because I have repeated this sentence to myself about a hundred times since:

"I don't think I've ever seen you look like this, actually. You look really good."

Six years she has known me, and she had never seen me look like this.

Because I had never let myself.

Then she asked whether they made it in November, the baby's month.

At four the shower ended. I hugged everyone. I hugged Rachel. I hugged Paul. I drove home with the windows down.

I texted Donna from the driveway.

"Nothing got in. Not even her mother. Thank you."

She texted back: "I told you."

Then: "Did Rachel say anything?"

Me: "She asked me where I got it. And whether they make it in November."

A long pause. Then a smiley.

Rachel sent me a photo last week. Her knot arrived, with a little golden heart, November. The baby is due at the end of the month, and the christening will be in the spring.

For the first time in six years, I already know exactly what I'm wearing. And Lily's is in my dresser, in its box, waiting.

Twelve months of a shut jewelry box.

One small silver knot.

The birthday present I gave my 9-year-old granddaughter was taken away by her mother that same week. 

When I asked her why, she explained how my innocent gift could put my granddaughter's life at risk.

So I'm writing this for every grandmother who loves her grandkids as much as I love mine — to warn you about a common gift that I now know can put your grandchild in danger…

What I'm talking about is a necklace. But not just any necklace. A very specific kind that has become so common among little girls in the last few years that you probably wouldn't think twice about buying one. 

I didn't…

And what my daughter explained to me afterward is something I think every grandmother needs to hear before the holidays comes around this year.

Let me start from the beginning.

My granddaughter Maddie turned 9 in April. For months leading up to her birthday, she had been begging her mother, and me, and pretty much anyone who'd listen, for one very specific gift. 

Every single one of her friends at school had one. Her cousin had one. Two of her friends at dance class had one. 

She'd been asking every time I came over, "Grandma, please, PLEASE, for my birthday."

What she wanted was a NAME necklace.

A little gold chain with her name spelled out across the front. She'd shown me pictures on her mom's phone. There are hundreds of variations. Cursive. Block letters. Rose gold. Silver. Some of them come with little birthstones next to the name. She wanted one with her name written in cursive — MADDIE — in delicate gold letters.

I thought it was the sweetest thing in the world.

I remember thinking, "This is such a wholesome, innocent thing to want." A little girl who wants to see her own name on a chain around her neck like the grown-up ladies do. 

What could be more harmless than that?

So I ordered one. Beautiful little gold chain with "MADDIE" in cursive. Not too expensive, not too cheap. 

Sat in a little velvet box for a month waiting for her birthday.

She opened it on her birthday and I have never seen her light up like that in my life. She screamed. She ran across the room and threw her arms around my neck and told me it was the best present she'd ever gotten. She put it on in the middle of the party and wore it for the rest of the day.

I felt like the best grandmother in the world.

Then that weekend, I went over to my daughter's house to drop off some leftovers. Maddie was in her room. I could tell something was wrong the second I walked in. She was sitting on her bed with her arms crossed, sulking. Her mother was in the kitchen and I could tell there had been an argument.

I sat down on her bed and asked her what was going on.

"I'm mad at Mom."

"Honey, what happened?"

"She took my necklace away. The one YOU gave me."

I asked her why. She didn't know. She just knew her mother had told her she couldn't wear it anymore and had put it in a drawer.

Now I want to tell you the truth about how I felt in that moment. I was hurt. A little bit angry, if I'm being honest. 

That was MY gift. My granddaughter had loved it. And her mother had taken it away without even asking me. I walked into the kitchen fully ready to have a difficult conversation with my own daughter.

She was standing at the sink. Before I could say anything, she turned around and looked at me and said, "Mom. Sit down. I need to tell you something."

She'd been waiting to talk to me.

She sat me down at the kitchen table and pulled up her phone. She showed me one article. Then another. Then a Facebook post from a mother in her own group of friends. 

Then a Reddit thread where women were sharing what had happened to their daughters.

Stories about strangers approaching little girls in public and acting like they knew them because they'd read the name off the necklace.

I realized the danger in real time at that table, and I felt sick to my stomach. 

I hadn't known. I want every grandmother reading this to hear me:

I HAD NOT KNOWN. I'm 71 years old. 

I wore my name on a chain when I was a teenager in the 1970s.

It never once occurred to me that the world had changed. 

It never once crossed my mind that a name on a little girl's neck in 2026 means something completely different than it did back then.

I thought I was giving my granddaughter something sweet. And I had almost put her in danger.

My daughter was so kind about it. She hugged me. She said, "Mom, of course you didn't know. Most people your age don't know. 

That's why I wanted to explain it to you and not just take it away without saying anything."

But I still felt stupid. I felt so, so stupid.

I drove home that day and I sat at my own kitchen table for a long time. 

I thought about Maddie's face when she opened that necklace. 

I tried to think of something else. I looked at initial necklaces. 

I looked at little heart pendants. I looked at birthstones. 

Nothing felt right, and every time I brought one up, Maddie was polite but I could tell it wasn't what she'd wanted. 

She'd wanted her NAME. 

Because that was what her friends had. That was what she'd been dreaming about for months.

Then one Sunday after church, a woman I've known for 15 years — she sits in the pew behind me every Sunday, and I'd told her the whole story over coffee more than once — she pulled me aside and said, "Have you heard of Tulas?"

I hadn't.

She reached under her collar and pulled out a beautiful gold chain. It looked like a delicate little beaded necklace. 

Tiny gold beads, some round, some like little bars, all along a thin gold chain. There was no name on it. No engraving. No letters. Just beads.

She said, "Guess what mine says."

I looked at it. I had no idea.

She said, "It says my husband's name. In Morse code. 

Every bead is either a dot or a dash. The combinations spell out letters. Only I know what it says."

I stared at her necklace for a long time.

Because I finally saw what I'd been looking for. 

A name necklace with my granddaughter's REAL name on it — her actual name, not an initial, not a substitute, not a heart charm — that no stranger in the world could read. 

She could wear it to school. To dance. To the store. And nobody, nobody, would ever be able to call her by name off of it.

I went home and ordered one that afternoon. 

14-karat gold-filled. "MADDIE" encoded in Morse code across the beads. 

It arrived in a beautiful little gift box with dried flowers inside about a week later.

I drove to my daughter's house and gave it to Maddie on a Sunday. I told her the beads on this necklace spell her name in Morse code. 

That nobody in the world can read it unless she wants to tell them. 

That she can wear it every day and it's her secret and only hers.

She threw her arms around my neck the same way she did on her birthday. Put it on right there in the living room. Hasn't taken it off since.

My daughter cried when she saw her put it on. She said, "Mom, this is the one she can wear."

That was five months ago. 

Maddie wears that necklace to school every single day. To dance. To sleepovers. 

To the pool. She showers in it. She sleeps in it. It's 14-karat gold-filled, so it doesn't tarnish or fade — it's designed to be worn every day and never come off. 

That's exactly how she wears it.

And every single day I know one thing. She's wearing her name on her chest, and nobody in public can read it.

If you have been thinking about a name necklace for your granddaughter — or your daughter, or your niece, or any little girl you love — please, before you order one from Amazon or Etsy or a mall kiosk, go to Tulas.co.

Betty White didn't have a single relationship for 40 years after her husband died in 1981.

You won't believe what she wore around her neck for all those years.

I was Betty White's personal assistant for 22 years.

I came on in 1999. Allen had already been gone 18 years by then. I was in that house until the morning the house went quiet in December of 2021. I woke her up most mornings. I drove her to set. I handled her mail. I was the one who called her sister. I was the one who closed the door of her bedroom for the last time.

She hired me because I didn't ask questions, which I think is the main qualification for working for anyone who has been famous for 70 years. She kept me because I didn't lie, which is the main qualification for working for anyone who has been grieving for 40.

I am telling you about a necklace. But first I have to tell you about her bedroom.

America thought it knew Betty White. The jokes. The vodka. The hotdog on The Tonight Show. The woman who was 85 on Saturday Night Live and funnier than any of the kids. For 50 years the country wrote her a part — the sweetest woman in Hollywood who was also the dirtiest — and she played it perfectly, right up to the end.

What the country didn't know was her bedroom.

On the nightstand to the right of the bed, in a small silver frame, was a photograph of Allen Ludden. Not the famous Allen. Not Password Allen. A quiet Allen in a cardigan on a dock, around 1979, 2 years before he died.

Every single morning for 22 years, I watched her lean over, blow a kiss toward that frame, and say good morning to him before her feet hit the floor.

She did it when she was 77. She did it when she was 99. She did it the morning before her last Christmas. I have watched her do it in a wig and I have watched her do it with the flu and I have watched her do it with 2 writers waiting in the kitchen. It was the first thing that happened in her day. It was not optional.

Allen's photo wasn't the only thing in her bedroom that was still his.

The closet had 2 of his sweaters still hanging in it. A grey one and a navy one. The sleeves had gone soft in a way sleeves only get after 40 years of a woman holding them.

In the drawer under the sweaters there was a stack of Tupperware containers. 4 of them. His shirts, sealed. She told me once, in the only sentence she ever said to me on the subject, that his smell was in the fibers and she wasn't ready to lose it. She was 93 at the time. She was not ready to lose it.

On the dresser there was a small velvet box. Inside was Allen's wedding ring on a thin gold chain. She wore it on their anniversary, on his birthday, on the day he died, and on Christmas Eve. 4 days a year. The rest of the year it stayed in the box.

And then there was the chain she never took off.

A thin gold chain. Delicate. A pattern of tiny gold beads and little lines spaced along it. If you saw it in a photo you'd think it was something a granddaughter had given her at Christmas. Easy to miss.

She wore it in her nightgown. She wore it in the shower. She wore it under the collar of every outfit the wardrobe people put on her for 22 years. She slept in it. The one time I saw it off her body in all those years was the week she had surgery in 2017, and even then it was in a little plastic bag taped to her chart.

She reached for it constantly. When she was reading a script. When she was listening to someone on the phone she didn't want to be listening to. When she was quiet in the car. Her thumb moved across the beads, one at a time, slowly, like she was counting them. She didn't know she was doing it.

For 22 years I assumed it was something Allen had given her early. I had a story in my head about an anniversary dinner in the 70s and a small box and a chain she just preferred over everything else in the drawer. I never asked, because it felt rude, like asking about her wedding ring.

I found out what it actually was the week after she died.

Her goddaughter and I were in the Carmel house packing up the bedroom. We'd been crying off and on for 3 days. We were doing the dresser.

An older woman from CBS came by to pay her respects. She'd worked with Betty since the Password days. Hair and makeup for 50-plus years. She was 84 and sharp and she sat down on the edge of the bed and looked at the dresser and asked us if we'd found the little chain.

I told her yes. We'd put it in a small box with the ring.

She said, "You know that isn't just a necklace, don't you?"

I said I'd always figured it was something Allen gave her.

She shook her head. And then she reached up to her own collar, and pulled out a fine gold chain of her own. Same little beads. Same little lines.

She said, "It's Morse code. The beads are dots. The lines are dashes. Hers spelled 3 words. Betty had this made the year after Allen died, and she wore it every single day for 40 years."

She was quiet for a second.

Then she said the 3 words.

Good morning Allen.

That is what the chain spelled.

Good. Morning. Allen.

The exact words she said to the photograph on the nightstand every single morning for 40 years.

She had been saying good morning to Allen out loud for 10 seconds a day. She had been saying it in a code against her chest for the other 23 hours and 59 minutes.

I sat down on the floor of the bedroom and I cried for the third time that week. Because I had worked for her for 22 years and I had been in that bedroom thousands of times and I had never once put it together.

The older woman told me Betty couldn't do what other widows did. She couldn't wear black. She couldn't cry at the grocery store. She couldn't let the grief show, because America had decided Betty White was going to be the sweet one, the funny one, the one who was fine. She had to be on a stage 2 months after she buried him. She had to make the country laugh at Allen's old show when she couldn't even watch it alone in the house.

"She needed something she could wear in front of all of it," the older woman said. "Something so she didn't have to be the sad widow everyone tiptoes around. One sentence. His sentence. In a code nobody could read."

She asked me, carefully, if I knew where Betty had gotten hers.

I didn't.

The older woman told me the name. Tulas. A small company. They hand-code any name, any word, any phrase, up to 22 characters, into Morse code along a fine gold chain. From the outside it looks like an ordinary necklace. Nobody in the world can read it but the person wearing it.

I looked them up that night in a hotel room in Carmel. I had braced for the kind of number a Betty White piece would cost. I was ready for 4 figures.

It cost less than a full tank of gas.

14K gold-filled. Waterproof. Doesn't tarnish, doesn't fade. The clasp is tight. The beads are set so nothing slips off. The chain adjusts while it's on. You put it on once and never take it off. Over 101,000 orders filled.

Which mattered to me, because I was already thinking about who I was ordering it for.

My father died 7 years ago. 42 years of marriage and then a stroke. My mother is the strongest woman I know, and she has spent 7 years doing exactly what Betty did. She has held it together for everyone. She has never once worn a memorial anything. When I asked her why, she told me she didn't want to be the sad widow everyone tiptoes around. She didn't want that to be the first thing people saw when she walked into a room.

I understood her completely. And now there was finally something I could do about it.

I ordered one with his first name on it. William. And the day they got married.

It came in a beautiful little box. I brought it to her kitchen on a Sunday and set it on the counter and told her she could open it when she wanted. She opened it right there in front of me.

She lifted the chain out and waited for me to explain what she was looking at. So I told her. The beads and lines were Morse code and it spelled Dad's name and the day they got married. Nobody in the world would ever know what it said. She could wear it anywhere, and no one would ever look at her with that face. The sad one. The one she hates.

She held it against her chest with both hands and my mother, who had not cried in front of me in years, cried in her kitchen for 10 minutes.

She put it on that night. She has not taken it off since. My aunt saw it and ordered one for her own late husband. My mother-in-law ordered 2 more.

Every one of them said the same thing when the box arrived.

Why did nobody tell me about this sooner.

Here's what I think about now.

For 22 years I was in the room while a 99-year-old woman said good morning to a photograph. I thought that was the ritual. The whole ritual. I thought I had the full picture.

I didn't. There were 2 rituals in that bedroom. One of them lasted 10 seconds. The other one lasted 40 years, every second of every day, out in front of every camera that ever pointed at her, in a code nobody but Betty could read.
